newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end mostly lower after data, supply.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end mostly lower after data, supply.

text.p: U.S. Treasury securities ended mostly lower under the weight of new supply and strong economic data, although quarter-end reshuffling elevated the front end of the curve, analysts said.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond closed off 6/32 at 95-17/32, yielding 6.98 percent. The yield curve shifted little, with the two-year note closing unchanged at 99-26/32 to yield 6.35 percent.
Only the bill sector posted gains, with the 3-month bill leading the way with a five-basis-point rate decline.
"Essentially we've come back, at least in the near term, to equilibrium," said Lee Youngdahl, bond market analyst at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co. "We don't have too many longs and too many shorts."
Before recovering to closing levels, prices were down by half a point in mid-afternoon, because dealers dumped the newly minted five-year notes they had just bought, players said.
The Treasury sold $12.5 billion of five-year notes at a yield of 6.66 percent, below the expected 6.67 percent yield.

Most dealers had short positions going into the auction and placed their bids "cavalierly," one trader said. In that scenario, the Dutch auction left dealers paying perhaps more than they should have, he said.

In selling off, the market exhibited "post-auction nervousness at a lack of follow-through interest," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A. Inc. "A lot of people were sitting on new positions and somebody just kind of panicked."
Cash bonds and futures sold lower until a large buyer of five- and 10-year paper stepped in, Stiles said.
By then, the June bond contract was down to about 108-6/32. It only briefly pierced the 108-8 level corresponding to a 7.00 percent bond yield, which some analysts had seen as near-term support.

"Seven (percent) has been the barrier for the last couple of weeks," said John Park, an economist at Sanwa Securities (USA) Co. "We pushed above it for a little while today, but then we dropped back down."
In T-bills, typical end-of-quarter flows rolled in throughout the session.
"There was very good buying, including retail buying, in the shorter bills and that gave a bid to three-month paper," one trader said.
He projected six- and 12-month bills would catch a favorable bid on Thursday since they were slow to appreciate on Wednesday.
"We could do a lot better," he said. "I don't know if three-months will, but you could do a lot better in six-months and yearbills."
A stronger-than-expected durable goods report set the bearish tone for the day, reversing slight early gains.
Durables orders jumped 1.5 percent in February, playing to market fears of swift economic growth and further rate hikes.
More broadly, six-month bill rates were off 4/32 at 5.33 percent, and one-year bills were unchanged at 5.57 percent.
The five-year note was off 1/32 at 98-10/32 to yield 6.66 percent, and the 10-year was off 4/32 at 96-6/32 to yield 6.78 percent.
PSA The Bond Market Trade Association has recommended an early close at 1400 EST/1900 GMT on Thursday and a full close on Friday.
